```{r setup}
library(bssd)
```

## Introduction

The safety of a study drug is often monitored while the treatment
assignment of an ongoing trial is still blinded. The blinded data show the
adverse events of special interest, but not the treatment groups of the
subjects. bssd computes the posterior probability that the risk of the event
is higher on the study drug than on placebo (control) from such data, with
published Bayesian methods. Several of these methods were computed by Markov
chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. bssd computes all posterior distributions
by numerical integration, so the results do not depend on a random seed, and
they are fast enough for simulation studies of the operating characteristics
(`sim_oc()`).

## Models and functions

| Model | Function | Blinded data | Tested quantity | Article |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BDRIBS(1) (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2018; Duncan, 2026) | `bdribs_post()` | number of subjects with the event and total exposure time | rate ratio | `vignette("bdribs1")` |
| BDRIBS(2) (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2018; Duncan, 2026) | `bdribs_post()` | number of subjects with the event and total time at risk | rate ratio | `vignette("bdribs2")` |
| BINBETA (Ball and Schnell, 2016) | `binbeta_post()` | numbers of subjects and of subjects with the event | study drug proportion or ratio | `vignette("binbeta")` |
| MULTIBIN (Goren et al., 2020) | `multibin_post()` | the same, for each of several studies | common rate ratio | `vignette("binbeta")` |
| CANARY (Gould and Wang, 2017) | `canary_post()` | total event count, with external control data | ratio, difference or odds ratio | `vignette("canary")` |
| EXP_BERN (Duncan, 2026) | `expbern_post()` | event indicator and follow-up time of each subject | rate ratio | `vignette("expbern")` |
| LL_BERN (Duncan, 2026) | `llbern_post()` | event indicator and follow-up time of each subject | ratio of the cumulative incidences at `t_star` | `vignette("llbern")` |
| EXPTIME (Schnell and Ball, 2016) | `exptime_post()` | number of events and follow-up time of each subject | study drug rate or rate ratio | `vignette("exptime")` |
| MAPBERN (Brock et al., 2023) | `mapbern_post()`, `map_beta()` | event indicator and time at risk of each subject, historical control arms | ratio of the event probabilities | `vignette("mapbern")` |
| BDRIBS monitoring (Waterhouse et al., 2022) | `bdribs_grid()`, `pooled_ratio()` | as BDRIBS, for grids of data and pooled trials | rate ratio | `vignette("bdribs-monitoring")` |

Each article describes the model and its numerical integration, with
examples and comparisons with MCMC or with the published results.

The study drug and placebo are randomized in the ratio $k:1$. The models
differ in what they assume about the treatment assignment. In EXP_BERN,
LL_BERN, BINBETA, MULTIBIN, EXPTIME and MAPBERN, each subject is on study
drug with probability $k / (k + 1)$ (simple randomization); in BDRIBS the
exposure is divided between the arms in the ratio $k:1$, and in CANARY the
arm sizes are fixed at their expected values (Gould and Wang, 2017). The prior of the placebo parameters must be informative in all
models (for example, from historical placebo data), because the blinded
data alone do not separate the two arms.

A signal is declared when the posterior probability that the tested
quantity exceeds its critical value is larger than a threshold, for example
$P(RR > rr_0 \mid \mathrm{data}) > \mathrm{cutoff}$ for a relative risk
$RR$. The defaults are $rr_0 = 1$ and $\mathrm{cutoff} = 0.95$. BINBETA,
EXPTIME and MAPBERN can instead test the study drug proportion or rate
against a critical value.

`signal_count()` gives the smallest event count with a signal for a number
of subjects (the boundaries of Ball and Schnell, 2016, and the control
charts of Gould and Wang, 2017), `count_oc()` the exact probability that the
count reaches it, and `elicit_prior()` the parameters of a prior from two
quantiles.

## Example with aggregate data

Hypothetical example 2 of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018, Section 4.4) has a 2:1
randomization, a background event rate of 0.011 per patient-year on placebo,
and 540 patient-years of blinded exposure. The BDRIBS model sets the prior
of the rate ratio $r$ through the probability $p = r k / (r k + 1)$ that a
subject with the event is on the study drug, with
$p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$ (`p_prior`; `vignette("bdribs1")`). The
screening analysis of the article treats the background rate as known,
which corresponds to `pt_hp = Inf`. With the uniform prior for $p$, the
posterior probabilities for 8 and 9 events are

```{r aggregate}
ex2 <- expand.grid(rr0 = c(1, 1.3), y = c(8, 9))
ex2$bssd <- mapply(function(y, rr0) {
  bdribs_post(y = y, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011, pt_hp = Inf,
              p_prior = c(1, 1), rr0 = rr0, details = FALSE)$prob
}, ex2$y, ex2$rr0)
ex2$published <- c(0.622, 0.434, 0.756, 0.584)
knitr::kable(ex2[, c("y", "rr0", "bssd", "published")], digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Events", "rr0", "bssd", "Mukhopadhyay et al."))
```

The published values were computed by MCMC with the bdribs package, and they
differ from the values of bssd by at most
`r signif(max(abs(ex2$bssd - ex2$published)), 1)`. The print method
summarizes the posterior with 9 events:

```{r aggregate-print}
fit9 <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                    pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1))
fit9
fit90 <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                     pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1), level = 0.90)
```

The posterior mean of $r$ is `r round(fit9$rr[["mean"]], 2)`, and the
article reports 1.53. The article gives (0.52, 2.83) as the 95% interval of
$r$. This agrees with the equal-tailed 90% interval,
(`r round(fit90$rr[["lower"]], 2)`, `r round(fit90$rr[["upper"]], 2)`),
which `level = 0.90` gives, and the equal-tailed 95% interval is
(`r round(fit9$rr[["lower"]], 2)`, `r round(fit9$rr[["upper"]], 2)`).

## Example with subject-level data

The following data are simulated with `sim_blinded()` under the placebo
distribution and the largest study drug distribution of scenario 6 in
Table 1 of Duncan (2026). The 150 subjects are randomized 1:1, they enter the
trial uniformly over 26 weeks, and each subject is followed for up to 104
weeks. The time to the event has a log-logistic distribution with
$\sigma = 0.8$, for which the hazard first increases and then decreases. The
cumulative incidence at week 104 is
`r round(100 * ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8), 1)`% on placebo and
`r round(100 * ll_cdf(104, mu = 5.85, sigma = 0.8), 1)`% on the study drug.
The blinded analysis is at week 117, the third interim analysis in the
simulations of the folder `reproduce` of the installed package.

```{r subject-data}
set.seed(2026)
d <- sim_blinded(n = 150, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 104,
                 analysis_time = 117, dist = "loglogistic",
                 par_p = c(7.3, 0.8), par_d = c(5.85, 0.8))
head(d[, c("id", "entry", "follow_up", "event", "event_time")])
tar <- time_at_risk(d$follow_up, d$event, d$event_time)
tar
```

The column `group` of `d` holds the true treatment group, which the blinded
analyses do not use.

The data are analyzed with the four models of Duncan (2026). Their priors
of the placebo parameters are based on historical placebo data with the
event rate $\lambda_{HP}$ and the total patient time $PT_{HP}$, discounted by
the factor $DF$. The priors follow the simulations in the folder
`reproduce`: a historical placebo group of 75 subjects, the size of the
current placebo group, followed for 104 weeks and discounted by $DF = 2$.
For BDRIBS and EXP_BERN, $\lambda_{HP}$ is the constant hazard per week that
gives the placebo incidence at week 104, and $PT_{HP}$ is in patient-weeks.
For LL_BERN, the Gamma priors of $\mu_p$ and $\sigma_p$ have the means
`mu_hp` and `sigma_hp`, and `pt_hp` divided by `df_p` sets their precision.
The simulations use the historical patient time in patient-years for it.
For LL_BERN, the relative risk is the ratio of the cumulative incidences at
the time $t^* = 104$; Duncan (2026) does not state which relative risk is
used for this model, and `?llbern_post` describes this choice and the
priors.

```{r subject-fit}
lambda_hp <- -log(1 - ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8)) / 104
pt_weeks <- 75 * 104
fits <- list(
  BDRIBS1 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]], exposure = tar[["exposure"]],
                        k = 1, lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks,
                        df = 2, t_star = 104),
  BDRIBS2 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]],
                        exposure = tar[["time_at_risk"]], k = 1,
                        lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2,
                        t_star = 104),
  EXP_BERN = expbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1,
                          lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2,
                          t_star = 104),
  LL_BERN = llbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1, mu_hp = 7.3,
                        sigma_hp = 0.8, pt_hp = pt_weeks / 52, df_p = 2,
                        t_star = 104)
)
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, summary))
res$model <- names(fits)
knitr::kable(res[, c("model", "prob", "signal", "rr_median", "ip_placebo",
                     "ip_drug", "ip_difference")], digits = 3,
             row.names = FALSE)
sig <- res$model[res$signal]
```

The column `prob` is $P(RR > 1 \mid \mathrm{data})$. Models with a signal at
the threshold 0.95:
`r if (length(sig) > 0) paste(sig, collapse = ", ") else "none"`. The
relative risk is the rate ratio $r$ for the BDRIBS and EXP_BERN models and
$RR(104)$ for LL_BERN. The table shows its posterior median, because the
posterior mean of $r$ is infinite for EXP_BERN under the default
Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior of $p$ (see `?expbern_post`). The last three columns are
the posterior means of the cumulative incidences at week 104 and of their
difference. The true values are
`r round(ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8), 3)`,
`r round(ll_cdf(104, mu = 5.85, sigma = 0.8), 3)` and
`r round(ll_cdf(104, mu = 5.85, sigma = 0.8) - ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8), 3)`.

## Accuracy of the numerical integration

`bdribs_post()` integrates over one dimension with `stats::integrate()`.
The other functions use Gauss-Legendre and Chebyshev quadrature on a region
located by a coarse grid (`llbern_post()` in four dimensions,
`multibin_post()` and the Poisson likelihood of `canary_post()` in one, and
the others in two). With `control$check = TRUE`, the default, they repeat
the computation on a finer grid, return the finer result, and report an
estimate of the integration error of `prob`, for example for the data
above:

```{r error}
vapply(fits[c("EXP_BERN", "LL_BERN")], function(f) f$integration$error,
       numeric(1))
```

The number of nodes can be changed with `control`. `?llbern_post` explains
why the error estimate of LL_BERN is twice the difference between the two
grids. `sim_oc()` turns the check off by default to save time.

## Operating characteristics

`sim_oc()` simulates trials with `sim_blinded()`, applies the selected models
at each analysis, and returns the proportion of trials with a signal and the
posterior mean of the difference in the cumulative incidence. The example
below uses the BDRIBS models with 200 simulated trials to keep the run time
short; the column `se` is the Monte Carlo standard error of `prob_signal`.
The cumulative incidence at week 52 is 10% on placebo and 20% on the study
drug, 350 subjects enter over 26 weeks, and the analyses are at weeks 26, 52
and 78.

```{r oc}
rate_of <- function(ip, t) -log(1 - ip) / t
design <- list(n = 350, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 52,
               analysis_time = c(26, 52, 78), dist = "exponential",
               par_p = rate_of(0.10, 52), par_d = rate_of(0.20, 52))
oc <- sim_oc(n_sim = 200, design = design,
             models = c("BDRIBS1", "BDRIBS2"),
             priors = list(bdribs = list(lambda_hp = rate_of(0.10, 52),
                                         pt_hp = 175 * 52, df = 2)),
             t_star = 52, seed = 1)
knitr::kable(oc$summary[, c("analysis_time", "model", "prob_signal", "se",
                            "mean_ip_difference",
                            "mean_observed_difference")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The true difference in the cumulative incidence at week 52 is
`r round(oc$truth[["difference"]], 3)`. The column
`mean_observed_difference` is the mean difference between the proportions of
subjects with the event in the two groups at the analysis, computed from the
true group assignment. The scripts in the folder `reproduce`
(`system.file("reproduce", package = "bssd")`) run the simulations of
Duncan (2026) for all four models with 1000 trials per scenario.

## Reproduction and validation

The installed package contains the scripts and the results of the
reproduction of published results (folder `reproduce`) and of the comparison
with independent computations (folder `validation`). Each item is judged as
PASS (agreement within the tolerance), EXPLAINED (a difference whose reason
is registered), FAIL (a difference without a registered reason) or INFO (no
value to compare with). The numbers of items are

```{r validation, echo = FALSE}
count_judgements <- function(folder, pattern) {
  dir <- system.file(folder, "results", package = "bssd")
  files <- list.files(dir, pattern = pattern, full.names = TRUE)
  rows <- lapply(files, function(f) {
    j <- read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)$judgement
    n <- table(factor(j, levels = c("PASS", "EXPLAINED", "FAIL", "INFO")))
    data.frame(file = basename(f), PASS = n[["PASS"]],
               EXPLAINED = n[["EXPLAINED"]], FAIL = n[["FAIL"]],
               INFO = n[["INFO"]])
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}
judgements <- rbind(count_judgements("reproduce", "^reproduce_.*[.]csv$"),
                    count_judgements("validation", "^validate_.*[.]csv$"))
knitr::kable(judgements, row.names = FALSE)
```

The reproduction covers Table 1, the hypothetical examples and the operating
characteristics of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018), Table 1, Figure 1 and the
simulations of Figures 2 to 10 of Duncan (2026), and the published results
of Schnell and Ball (2016), Gould and Wang (2017), Brock et al. (2023), Goren
et al. (2020) and Waterhouse et al. (2022). Many simulation results are
INFO, because the articles do not report all settings of the simulations
and some published values are read from the figures. The validation
compares `bdribs_post()` with the bdribs package; the other posterior
functions with MCMC in JAGS (for `canary_post()`, with the Poisson
likelihood) and with independent Python computations (an exact finite
mixture for `binbeta_post()`); the default integration grids
with finer grids; and `sim_oc()` with an independent Python simulation. The
number of FAIL items is
`r sum(judgements$FAIL)`. The files
`README.md` and `results/SUMMARY.md` in each folder describe the scripts,
the tolerances and the reasons for the EXPLAINED items.

FDA IND reporting final rule. In J. Lin et al. (eds.), *Statistical

Cham. <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-42568-9_17>

Brock, K., Chen, C., Ho, S., Fuller, G., Woolfolk, J., McShea, C. and
Penard, N. (2023). A Bayesian method for safety signal detection in ongoing
blinded randomised controlled trials. *Pharmaceutical Statistics*, 22(2),
378-395. <https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.2278>

Duncan, B. (2026). Robust safety monitoring and signal detection using
alternatives to the standard Poisson distribution. *Journal of
Biopharmaceutical Statistics*, 36(2), 227-244.
<https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2024.2395532>

Goren, E., Lin, L.-A., Blaustein, R. O. and Ball, G. (2020). Bayesian
meta-analysis of safety outcomes using blinded clinical trial data.
*Therapeutic Innovation & Regulatory Science*, 54, 1557-1565.
<https://doi.org/10.1007/s43441-020-00183-7>

Gould, A. L. and Wang, W. B. (2017). Monitoring potential adverse event rate
differences using data from blinded trials: the canary in the coal mine.
*Statistics in Medicine*, 36(1), 92-104. <https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.7129>

Mukhopadhyay, S., Waterhouse, B., and Hartford, A. (2018). Bayesian
detection of potential risk using inference on blinded safety data.
*Pharmaceutical Statistics*, 17(6), 823-834.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.1898>

Schnell, P. M. and Ball, G. (2016). A Bayesian exposure-time method for

Waterhouse, B., Hartford, A., Mukhopadhyay, S., Ferguson, R. and

decision to refer an event for unblinded evaluation. *Pharmaceutical
